us_large_broad.rationale: Fact: with most companies reported, Q3 2026 S&P 500 blended EPS growth is 31.4% and revenue growth 14.3%. 84% beat EPS, but the average beat was only 2.7%, and analysts expect 28.4% growth in Q4 (FactSet, Nov 6). Fact: the S&P 500 fell 2.68% on the week, after a 4.4% drop on Nov 5, its worst day since April 2025. The Nasdaq entered a correction as AI and chip stocks sold off, partly on worries that the Democratic Congress will restrict data-center buildout. Interpretation: BofA described the drop as multiple compression rather than estimate cuts, and the forward P/E is now 17.7. That leaves strong earnings against higher volatility, tech-concentration risk and live December Fed-hike risk, so the net score is neutral.

us_small_mid_value.rationale: Fact: in the Nov 5 rout, Large Value (IVE) fell 2.80% and Large Growth (IVW) fell 5.75%. Over one month, IVE is +2.6% against IVW -11.6%, and Small Value (IJS) is up 16.2% year to date. The Russell 2000 fell 2.05% on the week, against -2.68% for the S&P 500. Fact: October ISM manufacturing rose to 55.5, and payrolls beat (+165k), which supports domestic cyclical earnings. Interpretation: rotation away from AI megacaps and firm domestic data favor value and mid-caps. December Fed-hike risk (roughly 70% priced before the jobs report) is the main headwind for leveraged small caps, so confidence is low.

us_factor_dividend.rationale: Fact: defensive and income sectors held up in the selloff. On Nov 5, Staples (XLP) fell 0.75% and Utilities (XLU) 0.71%, against 4.4% for the S&P 500. Over one month, XLP is +12.6%, Health Care +10.5% and XLU +8.3%. Fact: McDonald's raised its dividend 4% (Nov 4) and Lam Research authorized a $25B buyback; companies have authorized a record pace of buybacks in 2026, and November is typically the heaviest month for executing them (secondary source). Interpretation: the AI de-rating favors quality and dividend factors. The offsets are a 10-year yield near 4.86% and possible Fed tightening, which keep the tailwind mild.

financials.rationale: Fact: Financials (XLF) rose 1.15% on the week while the S&P 500 fell 2.7%. AIG beat Q3 estimates on 42.5% higher net investment income and 7% premium growth, but its combined ratio rose to 91.3% on convective-storm catastrophe losses. Fact: Democrats won the Senate (about 54 seats) and are projected to win the House, raising oversight and regulatory risk. The Fed is trying to finalize a capital-rule overhaul by year end, and Senate control limits the White House's ability to reshape the Fed. Interpretation: the curve is steep (2y 4.51%, 10y 4.86%) and the economy is firm, which helps net interest income. Higher regulatory risk from 2027 and catastrophe losses offset that, so the net reading is neutral.

regime_notes: Two forces dominated the week. First, the midterms gave Democrats the Senate (about 54 seats) and a projected House majority, which means gridlock with the White House from January and more oversight. Second, a violent AI and semiconductor de-rating on Nov 5: the S&P 500 fell 4.4%, the Nasdaq entered a correction and the VIX jumped more than 65% intraday, partly on fears of restrictions on data-center buildout. Fundamentals are strong. Q3 S&P 500 EPS growth is 31.4% blended with 84% beating, although the average beat is small, and the forward P/E has compressed to 17.7. Leadership rotated hard from growth to value, defensives and healthcare. Macro is hawkish: payrolls rose 165k, unemployment is 4.1%, ISM prices are 75.2 and oil is near $90-98, which keeps a December 9 Fed hike live (about 70% priced before the jobs report). October CPI and PPI next week are the key swing factor for multiples.
